extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of Restoration drama; playwrights and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical considerations for writing, dedicating, and staging Restoration-era plays (comedy), including originality, audience taste, prologues, dedication practice, and the role of actors and critics in a play's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that even when subjects or characters are imitated from earlier romances or novels, a work can be original if the author treats the subject in a new manner. Langbaine's criticisms (that characters are imitated from Scarron) are used to illustrate a failure to grasp this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of a play's failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the fault was in the play itself, or in the lameness of the action, or in the number of its enemies, who came resolved to damn it for the title, I will not now dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success or failure can come from multiple sources: the inherent quality of the text, the quality of the stage performance (action/acting), hostile critics or political/social enemies, or prejudice against aspects like the title. One should consider all these factors rather than assume a single cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicating plays (practice & propriety)
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of dedicating plays is as common and unjust, as that of desiring seconds in a duel. It is engaging our friends ... in a senseless quarrel where they have much to venture, without any concernment of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden criticises the common practice of dedicating plays as often unnecessary flattering, potentially burdensome to patrons, and socially risky. He contrasts this with classical precedent (Horace, Ovid), noting that some poets historically used dedications to honour friends and secure future reputation—but also implies a writer need not force friends to suffer for their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to patrons and the aim of dedicatory epistles
rubrics_metrics.description: I have chosen that poet to whom I would resemble you ... to be recorded in the number of those men whom you have favoured with your friendship and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicatory epistles can be used to secure favor, to associate oneself with respected contemporaries, and to gain testimony of friendship that will aid reputation with posterity. Classical examples (Horace & Ovid praising contemporaries) are given as models for this tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics, censure, and pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: They paint lewdness, atheism, folly, ill-reasoning, and all manner of extravagancies amongst us, for want of understanding what we are. Oftentimes it so falls out, that they have a particular pique to some one amongst us, and then they immediately interest heaven in their quarrel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism often springs from ignorance, malice, or particular spite rather than fair judgment. Authors should expect pedantic or malicious attacks and understand that such censure may reflect the critic's biases. Dryden counsels measured response rather than inflamed rejoinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance quality (action & actors) as determinant of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The lameness of the action ... the players were ashamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play's textual quality is not sufficient: the actors' skill, the vigor of the staging, and the liveliness of the action strongly affect reception. Poor acting or a limp stage presentation can cause a good text to fail; conversely, capable players can help salvage or elevate a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste and the popularity of buffoonery/fops
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have Mamamouchi ... The unnatural strained buffoon is only taking; No fop can please you now of God's own making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary audiences frequently prefer extravagant fops, buffoonery, spectacle, and nonsense songs. Playwrights aiming for popular success should observe which farces and types ‘hit’ the crowd and may be forced to adapt (or risk disobliging the audience by offering wit they dislike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and purpose of prologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologues, like bells to churches, toll you in With chiming verse, till the dull plays begin; ... You damned the poet, but cried up the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prologues function rhetorically to prepare or influence the audience, comment on their follies, defend the poet, and modulate reception. They can be playful, admonitory, or defensive and are part of the poet's strategy to manage public opinion before the play begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable borrowing vs. plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Till then, he borrowed from romance, and did translate ... Langbaine ... threatens to 'pull off Ravenscroft's disguise, and discover the politic plagiary that lurks under it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges widespread borrowing (translations, adaptations from romances) as common practice; accusations of plagiarism are historically contested. The distinction lies partly in treatment and presentation: translating/borrowing subject-matter is not necessarily criminal if handled with original treatment; claims of extempore authorship ('extempore' or 'currente calamo') are viewed skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Fortune in literary success
rubrics_metrics.description: I have had formerly so much success, that the miscarriage of this play was only my giving Fortune her revenge; I owed it her, and she was indulgent that she exacted not the payment long before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden acknowledges that chance and fortune play a role in an author's varying fortunes: past successes do not guarantee future ones, and some failures are simply the balancing of luck. Writers should be conscious of contingency in reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging and learning from predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: I honour Ben Jonson more than my little critics, because, without vanity I may own, I understand him better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is both honorable and strategically wise to acknowledge predecessors whom one admires and from whom one has learned. Criticism framed as improvement rather than mere detracting aligns the author with tradition while defending innovation.
